title: Osteoporosis Is Not Just a Women's Disease, Delhi Data Show Men at Risk
excerpt: A Delhi study of 808 residents over 50 found vertebral fractures in 18.8% of men, as doctors on World Osteoporosis Day urged earlier DEXA screening to prevent fractures.
body:
• In the Delhi Vertebral Osteoporosis Study of 808 residents over 50, vertebral fractures were found in 18.8% of men — about 19 in every 100 men — slightly higher than the 17.1% found in women.
  • Men over 50 with risk factors such as steroid use, diabetes, smoking or low body weight should ask a doctor about a DEXA scan plus spine imaging, not density alone.
  • A first vertebral fracture is linked to a fivefold increase in the risk of another fracture, which is why finding the first one matters.
  • An estimated 50 million people in India had low bone density as far back as 2013, and roughly two-thirds of spinal fractures worldwide are estimated to go undiagnosed.

Osteoporosis is routinely described as a women's disease. Delhi data point the other way. In the Delhi Vertebral Osteoporosis Study, researchers found vertebral fractures in 17.9% of 808 residents aged over 50 — and the prevalence was 18.8% in men against 17.1% in women, according to figures released on World Osteoporosis Day, October 20, by Guntur neurosurgeon Dr. Mohana Rao Patibandla of Dr. Rao's Hospital.

Mumbai orthopaedic surgeon Dr. Amyn Rajani made the same point in comments reported by Medicircle: nearly one in three women over 50 in India is affected, compared with one in five men, and men are diagnosed late because the condition is wrongly perceived as a women's disease.

Why spinal fractures are missed

A hip fracture forces a hospital visit. A vertebral fracture often does not. Dr. Rao's release notes that roughly two-thirds of spinal fractures worldwide are estimated to go undiagnosed, and that in Delhi women over 50, counting spinal fractures alongside bone-density results raised the share needing treatment from 35.7% to 46.5% — with bone density no lower in women who had fractures than in those who did not. A reassuring scan, in other words, does not rule out a collapsed vertebra.

"A hip fracture announces itself. A spinal fracture often does not," said Dr. Rao. "Patients tell us, 'I have had back pain for months,' or 'I have become shorter,' and it is dismissed as ageing or arthritis."

The warning signs are specific: sudden back pain after 50, loss of height, a stooped upper back, pain that eases when lying down, and any fracture after a minor fall. Coughing or stepping out of a bathtub can be enough in advanced osteoporosis, Dr. Rao said. Among patients admitted with a recent non-spine fracture, 51% had a previously undiagnosed vertebral fracture, even when bone density was normal.

What screening actually involves

The test at the centre of screening is the DEXA scan, which measures bone density in the hip and spine. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says the procedure typically lasts about 15-20 minutes, reports a T-score comparing bone density with peak bone density, and notes that nearly 1 in 5 women and 1 in 20 men over 50 in the United States are affected by osteoporosis. The CDC recommends screening for women aged 65 and older, and for women aged 50 to 64 with risk factors such as a parent who has broken a hip.

Indian doctors cited earlier, risk-based screening. Dr. Rajani called DEXA the gold standard and recommended routine screening after 40-45, especially for women, with blood tests for vitamin D, calcium and thyroid function. Dr. Rao advised anyone over 50 with warning signs, or younger people with risk factors, to ask for a density scan together with spine imaging. The full release is at EIN Presswire.

Prevention starts before 50

Bone mass peaks around the age of 30, so prevention cannot start at retirement. The recommendations are consistent: adequate calcium, protein and vitamin D, with supplements guided by blood tests; weight-bearing exercise such as brisk walking and strength training; no smoking and minimal alcohol; and fall-proofing the home. Dr. Rajani listed milk, curd, ragi, sesame seeds and almonds, and warned calcium alone is poorly absorbed without vitamin D and exercise.

What this means for diaspora families

For Indian-American readers, the Delhi numbers describe their parents' generation at home — and, increasingly, themselves. A man over 50 in the United States with a prior fracture, steroid use or height loss should raise a DEXA scan with his physician rather than wait, and families in India should treat persistent back pain in an older relative as a reason to book a scan, not only painkillers.

What's next

Osteoporosis is treatable once found, Dr. Rao said: medicines can strengthen bone and cut the risk of the next fracture, while most spinal fractures heal with pain control, bracing and rehabilitation. The gap is detection. Until spinal imaging is routinely paired with density scans, the Delhi pattern — one in six older adults carrying a fracture nobody has named — is likely to persist.
